\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{booktabs}
\usepackage{hyperref}

\title{Neighbourhood Green Space and the Health Effects of
Extreme Heat: Evidence from Outpatient Records}
\author{M.~Wang and Q.~Chen}
\date{June 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Using six summers (2019--2024) of outpatient and emergency
records linked to community-scale green space coverage in a
large Chinese city, this paper examines how neighbourhood
green exposure moderates the health effects of extreme heat.
We find that community green coverage is significantly
negatively associated with heat-day outpatient visits,
and that the protective effect is stronger in communities
with a high share of elderly residents.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Rapid urbanisation has altered the surface energy balance, and
the frequency and intensity of extreme heat events have risen
markedly over the past two decades, with the urban heat island
further amplifying the threat that heat poses to residents.
Heat exposure is closely linked to acute episodes of
circulatory and respiratory disease, and the elderly, outdoor
workers, and chronic patients are the most vulnerable groups.
Green space is widely regarded as a key element of the built
environment for mitigating heat exposure, and its evaporative
cooling and shading effects are well documented at the
microclimatic scale.
Epidemiological evidence linking green exposure directly to
population health outcomes remains comparatively limited,
however, particularly at the community scale using routine
outpatient data.
Existing studies have largely focused on mortality or on single
heat-wave events, paying less attention to care-seeking
responses on ordinary hot summer days.
This paper uses six summers of outpatient records to examine
the relationship between community green coverage and
outpatient visits on extreme heat days, and tests whether the
relationship differs across communities with different
demographic structures.

\section{Data}
\subsection{Outpatient Records}
The outpatient and emergency data come from the municipal
health commission surveillance network, covering all visits to
43 secondary and tertiary hospitals during June--August of
2019--2024.
Records are aggregated by visit date and the patient's community
of residence into a community-day panel.
After excluding cross-city visitors and records with missing
addresses, the final sample contains 214 communities observed
over 552 summer days.

\subsection{Green Space Coverage}
Community green coverage is derived from 0.5 m resolution
remote-sensing imagery, computed as the share of vegetated
pixels within each community's administrative boundary.
Park green space, roadside planting, and residential
greenery are included, while water bodies and bare ground
are excluded.
Coverage varies substantially across communities: the mean in
the lowest quartile is only 11\%, against 43\% in the highest.

\subsection{Meteorological Data}
Daily meteorological data come from the municipal weather
bureau's surface station network, including daily maximum
temperature, mean humidity, and precipitation.
An extreme heat day is defined as a day with maximum
temperature above 35 degrees Celsius; 87 such days occurred
over the six years, concentrated between late July and
mid-August.

\subsection{Descriptive Statistics}
Table~\ref{tab:desc} reports community-level descriptive
statistics for the main variables.
Mean daily outpatient visits per community are 18\% higher on
extreme heat days than on other days, and the gap is visibly
larger in low-green communities.
Visits also display a strong day-of-week pattern, with Mondays
highest and weekends lowest, which the models absorb with
day-of-week fixed effects.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Variable & Mean & Std.\ dev. \\
\midrule
Daily outpatient visits per community & 312 & 158 \\
Green coverage (\%) & 27.4 & 12.6 \\
Share of residents aged 65+ (\%) & 14.8 & 5.3 \\
Built-up population density (1{,}000/km$^2$) & 18.6 & 9.1 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Descriptive statistics at the community level}
\label{tab:desc}
\end{table}

\section{Model Specification}
The baseline model is a negative binomial regression with
community fixed effects, where the dependent variable is the
community-day visit count and the key regressor is the
interaction between the extreme-heat-day indicator and green
coverage.
The models control for daily meteorological covariates,
day-of-week effects, and year effects, with standard errors
clustered at the community level.
Robustness checks vary the heat threshold and the visit-count
measure, and exclude days with anomalous air-pollution
monitor readings.

\section{Findings}
\subsection{Baseline Results}
The regressions show that, after controlling for built-up
density and demographic structure, every 10-percentage-point
increase in community green coverage is associated with an
average 4.6\% reduction in outpatient visits on extreme heat
days. % TODO: this conclusion needs two supporting references
The effect is insignificant on non-heat days, indicating that
the protective effect of green space operates mainly under
conditions of thermal stress.

\subsection{Heterogeneity Analysis}
Further analysis shows that the effect is significantly
stronger in communities with a high share of elderly residents:
in the top quartile of the 65+ population share, the visit
reduction from the same green increment reaches 7.9\%, about
three times that of the bottom quartile. % TODO: this comparison also needs literature support
A breakdown by disease category shows the largest reduction
for circulatory diseases, followed by respiratory diseases,
while injury visits are unrelated to green coverage.

\subsection{Robustness Checks}
Raising the heat threshold to 37 degrees Celsius slightly
enlarges the interaction coefficient without changing the
conclusions.
Replacing visit counts with visit rates, maximum temperature
with wet-bulb temperature, and a leave-one-summer-out
procedure all preserve the sign and significance of the core
result.
Excluding the 21 days with anomalous ozone monitor readings
leaves the estimates nearly unchanged.
As a placebo test, leading the heat-day indicator by 14 days
yields an insignificant interaction, indicating that the
baseline result is not driven by seasonal trends in visits.

\section{Discussion}
Our findings extend the cooling evidence on green exposure to
population health outcomes, suggesting that built-environment
interventions can serve as a low-cost complement to heat-health
risk management.
The stronger effect in elderly communities is consistent with
the age gradient of heat vulnerability and argues for
prioritising green provision in ageing built-up areas.
Mechanically, green space may act through microclimatic
cooling, the diversion of daytime activity to shaded spaces,
and the attractiveness of green areas for outdoor activity;
our aggregate data cannot separate the three channels.
From a policy perspective, inserting pocket parks and
converting idle plots in existing built-up areas may be a more
realistic incremental path than building large new parks.
The study is limited by exposure misclassification from using
residential address as a proxy, by the inability to distinguish
green quality and usage intensity, and by the fact that
outpatient data miss extreme cases of at-home deaths.
Future work could combine wearable-device exposure measurement
to separate the cooling effect of green space from its
physical-activity promotion effect.

\section{Conclusion}
Community green coverage is significantly negatively associated
with outpatient visits on extreme heat days, and the effect is
concentrated in communities with a high share of elderly
residents.
Against the backdrop of increasingly frequent heat events,
green space should be treated as part of the urban public
health infrastructure, and its spatial allocation should be
coordinated with the distribution of population vulnerability.
The next step is to extend the framework to extreme cold
events in winter and to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of
green interventions.
\end{document}
